summary: Missoula County approved a one-year, countywide pause on data center development -- Montana's first county-level moratorium. Distinct from the site-specific Krambu/Bonner Mill fight already tracked in this dataset, which the withdrawal of that project's land-use application preceded by days. [Update 2026-07-22: The vote was unanimous, with all 30 public commenters speaking in favor; the one-year interim zoning ban runs through 2027-07-08.]
objective: Pause countywide data center development for one year pending regulations

jurisdiction: Yellowstone County (legal challenge to citizen initiative)
summary: The Yellowstone County Commission directed the county attorney to seek a court determination on whether the citizen ballot initiative requiring voter approval of data centers (the response to Quantica's Broadview project, tracked elsewhere in this dataset) is legal. The county's own attorney cited precedent likely barring such an initiative. [Update 2026-07-20: The county has confirmed it filed suit in district court (citing Treasure County v. Edlund) seeking a declaratory ruling on the citizen initiative's legality; no judge has ruled yet. In parallel, the signature drive for the initiative continues, with roughly 3,000 of the ~16,650-17,000 valid signatures needed collected so far, ahead of the 2026-08-12 deadline.] [Update 2026-07-30]: Quantica has argued that petition signatures collected for the ballot initiative should not count while the county's legality lawsuit remains pending. On 2026-07-29, the County Commission tabled a proposed policy (26-91) that would have restricted signature-gathering on county property, after backlash that it appeared targeted at the data-center initiative drive. No court ruling has been issued yet on the initiative's legality, and no updated signature count is available.
objective: Determine legality of citizen initiative requiring voter approval of data centers

jurisdiction: Cheyenne (water contamination / discharge ban tied to Meta contractor)
summary: The Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities named Meta's contractor (Goat Systems LLC/Fortis) as the source of a rare bacterium contaminating the city's reclaimed-water system. The board banned fill-and-flush/closed-loop discharges from data centers and suspended the water-reuse program. Ties to Meta's roughly 715,000 sq ft, ~$800M Cheyenne data center campus.
objective: Identify and stop the source of reclaimed-water contamination linked to a Meta data center contractor

summary: After a Planning Commission 4-3 recommendation to approve, Marietta City Council tabled Prime Group Holdings' Powers Ferry Place rezoning -- a proposal to convert part of a 90,000 sq ft self-storage facility into an 18MW data center -- amid large public protests, and passed a moratorium on all new data center applications in the city through December 31, 2026.
objective: Block Powers Ferry Place data center rezoning and pause new Marietta data center applications

summary: The City of Lakeland released a proposed ordinance creating a temporary moratorium on data centers and large-load electric customers (over 50 MW/month); a public hearing was held July 6, 2026. The move follows Florida SB484, signed by Gov. DeSantis and effective July 1, 2026, which bars utilities from shifting data-center infrastructure costs onto small-business and residential ratepayers. [Update 2026-07-20]: The first public hearing on the proposed moratorium was held today, July 20, 2026, drawing a large crowd; the final vote has been rescheduled to August 3, 2026. [Update 2026-07-30]: Per 2026-07-28 reporting, the proposed moratorium would cover Lakeland Electric's entire service territory -- notably, roughly 40% of Lakeland Electric customers live outside Lakeland city limits. Commissioner Ashley Troutman has proposed exempting facilities of 25 MW or less from the moratorium. The final vote remains set for August 3, 2026.
objective: Establish a moratorium on new data centers and large-load electric customers in Lakeland

jurisdiction: Spartanburg County (Valara Holdings $2.8B data center lawsuit)
summary: The SC Environmental Law Center sued Spartanburg County and Valara Holdings, alleging a $2.8B data center already under construction was improperly classified as a 'minor' land development to bypass planning-commission review; a merits hearing is set for July 30, 2026. SELC separately asked the SC Public Service Commission to pause construction pending review, with a PSC hearing held July 13, 2026 in Columbia. County Council separately took a first unanimous vote toward its own one-year data center moratorium. [Update 2026-07-16]: SELC's petition to the SC Public Service Commission (Docket 2026-158-E) had its hearing on July 13, 2026 in Columbia; no ruling or outcome has been reported yet. A separate recusal motion against Commissioner H. David Britt (filed 2026-06-30) remains outstanding. The merits hearing on the county-court suit over the 'minor development' mischaracterization remains set for July 30, 2026. [Update 2026-07-20]: No ruling has been issued yet on either the PSC petition (Docket 2026-158-E) or the Commissioner Britt recusal motion -- both remain pending. Separately, Valara/NorthMark is seeking a South Carolina state air permit for 11 new gas turbines to power the project, with a public comment deadline of July 31, 2026; a protest was held at the Spartanburg County Courthouse on July 19, 2026 as part of a national day of action against data centers. [Update 2026-07-30]: Per SC PSC Docket 2026-158-E, Valara filed a Motion to Dismiss on 2026-07-27; oral arguments have been rescheduled for the third time, now to August 5, 2026. The county-court 'merits hearing' originally set for July 30, 2026 has no confirmed outcome as of this update.
objective: Force public planning-commission review of the $2.8B Valara Holdings data center in Spartanburg County

jurisdiction: Burgin City Council (annexation for hyperscale data center)
summary: Burgin City Council voted 3-2 to give first reading to an ordinance annexing farmland from Mercer County -- roughly doubling the town's size (pop. ~1,000) -- to enable a hyperscale data center project; a moratorium amendment failed. Second reading is set for July 20, 2026, with a Mercer County Planning & Zoning Commission hearing set for July 23, 2026. Shaker Village CEO Billy Rankin publicly opposed the annexation, citing incompatibility with the area's tourism and heritage economy. The move comes despite Mercer County's own existing data-center moratorium (passed March 2026), which the annexation could effectively route around. [Update 2026-07-16]: Three new developments (2026-07-13 to 07-16): (1) The Mercer County Fiscal Court voted unanimously on July 14, 2026 to direct the County Attorney to draft a data-center moratorium (motion by Magistrate Susan Barrington); it would apply only to the unincorporated county and would become void once the Harrodsburg-Mercer Joint Planning & Zoning Commission's data-center ordinance is in place. (2) The Harrodsburg City Commission, at its July 13, 2026 meeting, authorized its city attorney to draft a formal objection to Burgin's annexation, alleging Burgin failed to give Harrodsburg the required 14-day notice, since Harrodsburg holds a water-line easement/water contract crossing the annexation properties. (3) Burgin City Council canceled its regular July 14, 2026 meeting; the second reading of the annexation ordinance remains set for a special meeting on July 20, 2026. [Update 2026-07-20]: Burgin canceled the planned July 20, 2026 special meeting (announced 2026-07-16); the city's own statement said the meeting "was not legally accurate as we have not had a first reading of the ordinance," meaning the annexation cannot legally proceed to a second reading -- contradicting earlier reporting of a 3-2 first-reading vote on July 9. No new meeting date has been announced. Harrodsburg's formal objection letter, dated July 14, 2026, was confirmed sent, citing the 14-day notice defect and an estimated ~$30 million cost to reroute Harrodsburg's water line around the annexation area. The Mercer County Planning & Zoning Commission hearing remains scheduled for July 23, 2026 (outside this window); written comments were due July 20, 2026. RESOLVED (2026-07-22): Burgin's own 2026-07-16 statement confirms no valid first reading of the annexation ordinance ever occurred, meaning the earlier-reported 3-2 first-reading vote on July 9 was inaccurate; the annexation cannot legally proceed to a second reading absent a new first reading. No new meeting date has been announced.
objective: Enable a hyperscale data center via Burgin annexation of Mercer County farmland

jurisdiction: Little Rock Board of Directors (hyperscale data center moratorium measure)
summary: A measure by City Directors Kathy Webb and Capi Peck to pause new hyperscale data center approvals through year-end was deferred to August 4, 2026 at the sponsors' request. As drafted, it would exempt the planned Google data center at the Port of Little Rock and only affect zoning applications in the 'hyperscale' category; the main opposition target is an AVAIO Digital project near Wrightsville in Pulaski County, alongside continued scrutiny of the Google Port project. UPDATE 2026-07-29: City Director Kathy Webb (Ward 3) is formally proposing to extend the halt from 6 to 18 months and to remove the earlier carve-out for the planned Google hyperscale facility at the Port of Little Rock. The proposal would require biannual public hearings with Entergy Arkansas and the developer present. Not yet voted on.
objective: Pause new hyperscale data center approvals in Little Rock through year-end

jurisdiction: Town of Warren (180-day data center moratorium)
summary: A special town meeting approved a 180-day data center moratorium in near-unanimous fashion, with about 60 residents attending -- nearly double normal turnout -- and the moratorium is renewable in further 180-day increments. No data center applications have been filed in Warren; the vote was preemptive, citing concerns about water and power use and potential river-temperature impacts.
objective: Pause data center development in Warren for 180 days, renewable

jurisdiction: Granville Township (emergency supervisors meeting on data center land development plan)
summary: Developer PA Data Center Partners filed a land development plan on 2026-07-10 for two parcels in Granville Township -- just two days before a special township meeting scheduled for 2026-07-12 to consider a data center moratorium, meaning the filing will be evaluated under existing zoning rather than any pending moratorium. An emergency supervisors meeting on 2026-07-14 drew roughly 100 residents opposing the project; supervisors opted to continue drafting a data center zoning ordinance rather than act immediately. The developer's announcement-stage figures (130-230 construction jobs, 150 direct plus 300 indirect permanent jobs, $22.5M in county tax revenue, $12.2M in school district revenue) come from the developer's own materials and are unverified. It could not be confirmed from available sources whether the ordinance was formally adopted at the meeting. A separate public town hall on the specific project is set for 2026-07-21.] [Update 2026-07-20: The 2026-07-21 town hall was postponed at PA Data Center Partners' own request (notice dated 2026-07-17), with no new date given. Adoption of Ordinance 2026-02 is still not confirmed -- the township's page shows it remains in the required PA Municipalities Planning Code review process.]

summary: Residents pressed the Nutley Board of Commissioners about an 11-acre parcel at the ON3 campus (the former Hoffmann-La Roche headquarters) that has been approved for data center use. Developer Prism Capital Partners settled a 2025 lawsuit that dropped a planned truck-terminal use and amended the redevelopment plan to permit a data center instead. summary: Alderman Richard Furlow introduced a 12-month moratorium ordinance on new data center development and conversions, scheduled for City Plan Commission review on 2026-07-15. The ordinance would convene a 6-month Department of Economic Development working group to recommend zoning standards for future data center development. [Update 2026-07-16: The City Plan Commission met on 2026-07-15 as scheduled to review the moratorium ordinance, but no outcome or vote had been confirmed by any source as of 2026-07-16.] [Update 2026-07-20: The ordinance has advanced to the Board of Alders' Legislation Committee, docketed for a public hearing on 2026-08-04 at 6pm. No direct reporting confirms what the City Plan Commission recommended at its 2026-07-15 meeting.]
objective: Pause new data center development/conversions in New Haven for 12 months pending zoning standards

summary: City Council approved a first-of-its-kind data center zoning ordinance for Wausau: restricts data centers to medium/heavy-industrial zones (none permitted by right), requires a conditional use permit with water/power/noise/light review by the Plan Commission, and mandates a minimum 200 ft separation from residential areas.

summary: Common Council advanced a pause on data center construction, directing staff to draft a formal moratorium ordinance. No project is currently proposed for the city, but a local petition opposing data centers had already attracted over 1,500 signatures; Council Member Alec Lefeber cited water, environmental, and quality-of-life concerns.
objective: Direct staff to draft a formal data center construction moratorium ordinance

summary: City Council voted 7-0 to pass a one-year moratorium on data centers and other 'high-impact utility consumers,' to allow a research study on localized water, power, farming, and climate impacts. Roughly 50 residents attended in support.
objective: Impose a 1-year moratorium on data centers and high-impact utility consumers pending a study

summary: City Council unanimously approved a 6-month moratorium on new data center construction applications, giving officials time to develop formal regulations. Per Zoning Administrator Jacob Holcomb, the city needs additional research time; the moratorium may be extended up to 12 more months or ended early once a permanent ordinance is adopted.
objective: Impose a 6-month moratorium on new data center construction applications

jurisdiction: Americus / Lyon County (Flint Hills Digital Campus), KS
summary: Americus City Council held a listening session on the proposed Flint Hills Digital Campus (developer Kanza Park Place; publicly described as a potential gigawatt-scale, roughly 1,000-acre data center campus west of Emporia) but took no formal action, explicitly declining to file any motion in order to prioritize public comment. Emporia Neighbors United founder Jay Vehige urged the city to take time and do thorough research; the group reported collecting nearly 1,850 signatures in the prior week opposing high-impact data centers and battery storage, up from roughly 1,400 signatures submitted July 8 that the Lyon County Clerk rejected as non-compliant with Kansas petition-witnessing requirements. The project remains at the announced/proposed stage with no permits issued. [Update 2026-07-17: Lyon County Commissioners approved a 10-day 'stopgap' freeze on new data-center and solar-farm permit applications (through Aug 1, 2026) and directed County Legal Counsel to draft a six-month moratorium for a vote at the commission's next regular meeting on 2026-07-24.] [Update 2026-07-19: Kansas Reflector investigative reporting found that Gary Pinkston — the public face of the Flint Hills Digital Campus — swore under oath in a federal bankruptcy proceeding that he has 'no interest at all' in the project and denied any relationship with Kanza Park Place LLC (the registered developer entity), which he said is owned by his daughters.]
objective: Halt new data center and solar-farm permits in Lyon County pending a six-month moratorium

A recall drive targeting the three dissenting commissioners launched the following day, 2026-07-14, reflecting continued community pushback against data center development in the county. The vote followed a packed public hearing at the county fairgrounds that drew applause from attendees opposed to data center development.
objective: Recommend a data center moratorium to the Cass County Board

summary: Alabama Citizens Against Data Centers held a protest at Railroad Park in Birmingham (roughly 40-50 attendees) on July 13, 2026, as part of a nationwide day of action affiliated with the Humans First campaign against AI data centers. Alabama gubernatorial candidate Doug Jones addressed the crowd, telling attendees "moratorium is the word," referencing ongoing fights over Nebius's BHM01 data center and Birmingham's data-center moratorium.
objective: Build public pressure for a statewide data center moratorium in Alabama

summary: Mayor James Solomon and the City Council introduced Ordinance 26-057 on first reading, which would ban data centers as a primary principal use in Jersey City's Industrial Districts. Roughly five existing downtown data center facilities would be grandfathered in under the ordinance. A final vote is scheduled for 2026-08-19.
objective: Ban data centers as a primary permitted use in Jersey City's Industrial Districts

summary: Tonawanda Seneca Nation, Sierra Club, and a Town of Alabama resident filed a lawsuit in Genesee County Supreme Court against the Town of Alabama, the Genesee County Economic Development Center (GCEDC), Stream U.S. Data Centers, and roughly 12 landowners, challenging the legality of the 2012 "Incentive Zoning Agreement" underpinning the STAMP tech park. The suit seeks to void the agreement and enjoin construction. This is a distinct action from the plaintiffs' earlier 2025 SEQRA-subsidy lawsuit over the same STAMP site.
objective: Void the 2012 Incentive Zoning Agreement underpinning the STAMP tech park and enjoin construction

summary: The Mercer County Fiscal Court voted unanimously on July 14, 2026 (motion by Magistrate Susan Barrington) to direct the County Attorney to draft a new data-center moratorium covering unincorporated Mercer County. The vote came amid the contested Burgin annexation of farmland for a proposed hyperscale data center (tracked separately) and is distinct from the county's existing March 2026 moratorium; the new measure would become void once the Harrodsburg-Mercer Joint Planning & Zoning Commission adopts a formal data-center ordinance. UPDATE 2026-07-28: The Fiscal Court gave unanimous first reading to the formal moratorium ordinance; second and final reading is set for August 11, 2026. The local group 'We Are Mercer County,' represented by attorney W. Henry Graddy, spoke in support at the reading.
objective: Draft a new moratorium on data centers in unincorporated Mercer County pending a joint zoning ordinance

summary: A July 16, 2026 Cincinnati Enquirer investigation found Amazon and Meta are each receiving millions of dollars in Ohio property-tax abatements for data center campuses in the New Albany corridor (Licking County), including Meta's 'Prometheus' cluster, with local officials described as 'still making deals.' No organized local-opposition action (moratorium, lawsuit, or contested vote) specific to Prometheus was found this window, in contrast to neighboring jurisdictions like St. Albans Township and Washington Township that have passed bans/moratoriums covering the broader New Albany data center corridor.
objective: Track local tax-abatement deals for Meta's Prometheus data center campus in the New Albany corridor

objective: Impose a 182-day moratorium on new data center development in Lansing, MI

No moratorium had been formally introduced or voted on as of 2026-07-14. This is Warren, Michigan (Macomb County) -- a different city and state from Warren, Ohio (Trumbull County), site of the Stargate Lordstown-area data center fight.
objective: Request a data center moratorium in Warren, MI after storm-related power outages

objective: Impose a 12-month moratorium on data centers and other energy-intensive development in Logan County, NE

The appeal was noted in a 2026 Marana election guide alongside other local issues; case details (plaintiff, specific grounds) were not confirmed in available reporting. Distinct from the separate Pima County/Beale Infrastructure 'Project Blue' rezoning tracked elsewhere in this dataset.

jurisdiction: Loudoun County (Spring Valley Tech Park public hearing)
summary: Loudoun County has scheduled a public hearing for July 23, 2026 on Active Infrastructure's proposal for a 362-acre, hydrogen-powered data center campus (reported at up to 1,300 MW) called Spring Valley Tech Park. The proposal follows a July 6, 2026 town hall hosted by Board Chair Phyllis Randall that drew hundreds of residents opposing continued countywide data center expansion. The megawatt figure is developer-reported and unverified against a primary filing. UPDATE 2026-07-30: The Board of Supervisors REJECTED Active Infrastructure's 3.25-million-sq-ft Spring Valley Technology Park rezoning on Evergreen Mills Rd. The Board also directed staff to prepare a September 15, 2026 agenda item pausing new data center applications, site plans, and substation applications countywide, along with a County Attorney legal analysis of whether such a pause is permissible under Virginia law.
objective: Community opposition to Active Infrastructure's 362-acre, hydrogen-powered Spring Valley Tech Park data center campus

summary: Surry County commissioners voted unanimously on July 21, 2026 to enact a two-year moratorium on new data center development, extending a prior 60-day pause. A steering committee will be formed to study community and infrastructure impacts before any new zoning framework is adopted.
objective: Pause new data center development in Surry County for two years pending an impact study

summary: The Southport Planning Board voted unanimously on July 16, 2026 to recommend the city adopt a 15-month moratorium on data center development rather than proceeding directly to a zoning text amendment, as city staff continue workshopping permanent zoning rules. The recommendation now goes to the Southport City Council for a final vote.
objective: Recommend a 15-month moratorium on data center development in Southport pending zoning rulemaking

A roughly 2,500-signature petition demands an immediate moratorium; about 150 residents attended a July 2026 commissioners meeting with roughly 40 speaking in opposition. No board vote has been taken yet.
objective: Demand an immediate moratorium on the PointOne Data Centers technology park project in Lee County over alleged deceptive framing

objective: Pause new data center applications in Cherokee County pending a longer-term moratorium decision

summary: Dougherty County commissioners approved a 45-day pause on new data center projects on July 20, 2026, amid rising regional concern about aquifer and grid impacts in the Albany area.
objective: Pause new data center projects in Dougherty County for 45 days

The Sowega Aquifer Alliance raised water-supply concerns during the session.

summary: A roughly 1,200-acre data center rezoning request near Brookwood Middle School is headed to an August 11, 2026 vote. The mayor denied a request to pause the process for a referendum. Black Warrior Riverkeeper has raised concerns about impacts to nearby waterways and endangered species.
objective: Oppose a 1,200-acre data center rezoning near Brookwood Middle School

summary: Neptune Township's Township Committee voted 3-1 on 2026-07-13 to ban both data centers and DHS/ICE immigration detention facilities townshipwide, becoming the 25th New Jersey municipality to ban data centers. The ordinance was developed in coordination with Climate Revolution Action Network NJ (CRAN), whose executive director Ben Dziobek said data centers are "driving up our utility bills, polluting our air, and using up all of our water." Neptune joins Andover Township, Millville, Red Bank, and Warren Township among NJ municipalities that have enacted similar bans.
objective: Ban data centers and ICE/DHS detention facilities townshipwide

opposition_groups: Falls Township Residents Against Data Centers
summary: A roughly four-hour public meeting was held on 2026-07-14 on Amazon's PA DEP air-quality plan-approval application for its 2-million-sq-ft "digital infrastructure campus" at Keystone Trade Center: 280 natural-gas-fired generator engines plus 3 diesel emergency generators. A petition seeking a 6-month freeze on new data center applications in the township has topped 3,800 signatures. Tensions ran high -- an Amazon representative's claim of improved air quality at a comparable Virginia facility drew boos, and neighboring mayors spoke in opposition. Amazon separately announced $150,000 in community grants, which some residents viewed skeptically amid the dispute. PA DEP's formal Notice of Intent for Phase 2 permit approval was set to publish 2026-07-18, opening a 30-day public comment period.
objective: Contest Amazon's air-quality permit application and press for a data center application freeze

project_name: Powder Mill Works data center campus
summary: S.S. Penn LLC -- an affiliate of Bethesda, MD-based developer Stonebridge Associates, which proposes a 15-building data center campus on 580 acres of the former Powder Mill Works property -- sued North Beaver and Mahoning townships over revised zoning ordinance amendments regulating data center siting, arguing its application was "administratively complete" before the amendments took effect and should be judged under the prior ordinance (the "pending-ordinance doctrine"). The townships' solicitor, Louis M. Perrotta, is moving to quash both lawsuits.
objective: Defend townships' revised zoning ordinances against developer's pending-ordinance-doctrine lawsuit

summary: Black Mountain — the Fort Worth-based energy consortium developing the separate $10B, 530-acre data center campus in southeast Fort Worth (see fort-worth-southeast-tx-2025-01-01) — purchased over 2,000 acres near Azle Highway and Pearson Ranch Road in unincorporated Parker County, about 7 miles northeast of downtown Weatherford, assessed at over $57 million per the Parker County Appraisal District. In April 2025 the TCEQ approved a related shell entity, Fort Worth Power Core LLC (Black Mountain CEO Rhett Bennett listed as CEO), to operate five natural gas turbines at 501 Pearson Ranch Road as “backup/bridge power for a new data center”; Weatherford's city manager said he wasn't told of the filing until a reporter asked, calling it “concerning.” The City of Weatherford declined to add data centers as an allowed zoning use on Jan 16, 2026 (“data centers will remain NOT ALLOWED in Weatherford”) and, after the Star-Telegram broke the land-purchase/TCEQ story on May 20, 2026, issued a follow-up statement criticizing the lack of public notice for the turbine permit; the property itself sits outside city limits, so Weatherford has no zoning authority over it. On June 9, 2026, the Parker County Commissioners Court held a standing-room-only special meeting and unanimously passed a resolution opposing large-scale data center development — specifically targeting high-volume open-loop water cooling — and committing to deny tax abatements to such projects, while acknowledging Texas counties have little formal land-use authority. Bennett has said Black Mountain is only “considering” a “potential” site here and disputes that Weatherford ever told the company it wasn't wanted; no source confirms the project has been formally committed or abandoned as of this writing.
issue_category: zoning; transparency; air_quality; water; grid_energy; noise; tax_incentive
objective: Prevent Black Mountain from siting a second hyperscale data center campus in Parker County near Weatherford

Commissioners declined to act on a citizen petition to prohibit data centers, which may instead go to a November ballot; a man was arrested at the meeting. This is a City of Emporia action, distinct from the Lyon County Commission's separate moratorium/listening-session process for the Flint Hills Digital Campus near Americus (see americus-lyon-county-ks-listening-session-2026-07-15).

objective: Pause new data center construction and development in Orangeburg County pending study

summary: A standing-room-only public forum was held ahead of an August 11, 2026 fiscal court vote on a data center moratorium. Judge-Executive Jason Marshall polled the room and reported near-unanimous opposition, citing a 1,500-person survey showing 80% opposed. No project is currently proposed for the county.
objective: Gauge public sentiment on data centers ahead of a county moratorium vote

summary: Falls Township's Board of Supervisors voted to declare portions of Chapter 209 of the zoning ordinance -- covering data-center districts, setbacks, noise, and water/power requirements, and the township's data-center definitions -- "substantively invalid" under the Pennsylvania Municipalities Planning Code's curative amendment process. The vote opens a 180-day window (to roughly late January 2027) for the township to rewrite data-center-specific zoning rules and shields it from developer validity challenges in the meantime. It does not halt the already-approved Amazon data center facility under construction in the township.
objective: Rewrite data-center zoning rules via curative amendment while shielding the township from developer validity challenges

summary: Cherry Hill Township Council voted unanimously on 2026-07-28 to ban large-scale data centers, designating them a non-permitted land use townshipwide while still allowing small in-house server rooms for local businesses. Any future data center proposal would need a zoning-board variance, described as one of the hardest land-use approvals to obtain. Mayor David Fleisher said "we don't think that Cherry Hill should be a guinea pig," citing the township's master-plan goals of preserving suburban character and natural resources. Cherry Hill joins Medford, Mansfield, Chesterfield, and Millville among South Jersey municipalities that have passed similar bans.
objective: Ban large-scale data centers townshipwide via zoning ordinance
